# `Markdown`

[Back to stdlib index](../stdlib.md)

Ipe.Markdown — render markdown source to `Ipe.Ui` Element trees.

Direct render-to-Element (no HTML string round-trip) so styling inherits
the surrounding theme (`Font.color`, `Background.color`, typography).
The output is a `Ui.column` of block-level elements — embed as a child of
any `Ipe.Ui` layout.

Supported subset — "chat-grade": enough for agent responses, commit
messages, PR bodies, and prompt history.

Block types: headers (# / ## / ### / #### / ##### / ######), paragraphs,
fenced code blocks (```), bullet lists (- / *), ordered lists (1.),
horizontal rules (---), tables (| ... | separator | ... |),
blockquotes (> …, nestable to 32 levels).

Inline: **bold**, *italic*, `code`, [text](url), ![alt](url) images,
trailing-double-space → line break.

Not supported (add when needed): footnotes, raw HTML pass-through, math,
mermaid.

Security: the parser never emits raw HTML, scripts, or event handlers —
every output routes through typed `Ipe.Ui` constructors. Link `href` and
image `src` become HTML attributes, which the runtime attribute sink
(`sanitise_url_attr`) validates as the single SSOT guard: it normalises the
scheme (stripping leading and intra-scheme control/whitespace, case) and
neutralises `javascript:`/`vbscript:`/dangerous `data:` schemes, allowing
only safe schemes and raster `data:image` URLs, so the output is HTML-safe
with no extra sanitisation step. (Compare: HTML-string renderers need a
sanitiser equivalent to bluemonday; this one does not.)

Bounds: parsing runs in time linear in the input's size, with a stack
bounded by the quote ceiling. Quotes nest at most 32 deep; text
quoted deeper renders as one flat paragraph. The caller bounds the input's
size.

Chrome colours (code surfaces, dividers, list markers, blockquote
left-rules) derive from the inherited theme foreground via `currentColor`,
so the render tracks a light or dark surrounding page with no fixed palette.

The parser is public: `parseBlocks` / `parseSpans` return the `Block` /
`Span` trees, so a caller wanting the parse but its own typography and
palette can walk them directly instead of reimplementing the parser.
